papers.abstract: We consider online prediction from experts, a fundamental problem in machine learning, under differential privacy constraints. Existing private algorithms achieve near-optimal regret $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$, where $T$ is the time horizon. However, this bound becomes suboptimal when $L^\star$, the cumulative loss of the best expert, is significantly less than $T$. In this work, we present the first differentially private algorithm with regret $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{L^\star})$, offering a substantial improvement in the low-loss regime. Our regret bound matches the non-private lower bound up to poly-logarithmic factors for constant privacy parameters, demonstrating that privacy incurs only a small cost in this setting. Our result assumes that the input sequence is oblivious, i.e., it is fixed in advance and independent of the algorithm's outputs. We also prove that an $\tildeΩ(\sqrt{T})$ regret is inevitable for adaptively generated inputs, even when $L^\star = 0$.
bullets: Addresses the gap between existing private regret bounds of ~O(√T) and easier low-loss cases.
Introduces the first private algorithm with regret ~O(√L⋆) for oblivious input sequences.
For constant privacy parameters, this matches the non-private lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors.
Shows that adaptive inputs necessarily incur ~Ω(√T) regret, even when the best expert has zero loss.
Scope: the improved low-loss guarantee assumes the sequence is fixed in advance and independent of algorithm outputs.
papers.selection_reason: Private online prediction from experts with improved small-loss regret; fits configured online-learning and adaptation interests.
papers.title: Private Online Prediction from Experts with Small Losses
papers.tldr: A differentially private online prediction algorithm achieves near-optimal regret scaling with the best expert’s loss, while adaptive inputs still require horizon-dependent regret.

papers.abstract: Merging different models into a single model is highly desirable for multi-task deployment, particularly in regulated domains like healthcare. In such settings, models are often locally fine-tuned due to strict data privacy policies, necessitating that aggregation operates exclusively on the fine-tuned weights. Existing methods apply a uniform merge across all tasks, ignoring the geometric relationships among their learned subspaces. When task updates occupy misaligned subspaces, projecting them onto a shared low-rank basis discards task-relevant directions, a failure mode named \emph{subspace interference}. Through this study, we show that the per-task projection error of a merged model is governed by the principal-angle alignment between each task and the shared subspace, so that grouping geometrically compatible tasks provably reduces this error within each group. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textbf{Group-wise Rank-Aware Model Merging (GRAM)}, which uses the principal-angle geometry of task vectors to decide which tasks should be merged together and then performs a standard SVD-based merge within each coalition; the pipeline requires only the fine-tuned weights at merge time. With only one additional model ($\nK{=}2$), GRAM significantly mitigates subspace interference and consistently outperforms prior merging methods across language understanding (GLUE with Flan-T5), 8-task CLIP vision, and medical instruction tuning (Qwen2-7B-Instruct with four English/Chinese medical LoRAs).
bullets: Uniform merging can cause subspace interference when task updates occupy misaligned directions.
Theoretical analysis links per-task projection error to principal-angle alignment with the shared subspace.
GRAM uses task-vector geometry to form compatible groups, then performs standard SVD-based merging within each group.
It requires only fine-tuned weights at merge time and uses one additional model (K=2).
The method consistently outperforms prior merging approaches across language, vision, and medical instruction-tuning settings.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are exact on small sets and drift into estimation on larger ones, a profile reminiscent of children before they master counting. Children cross the barrier with epistemic actions: pointing at each item while reciting number words, moving counted items aside, partitioning the array. We give VLMs the same actions as dumb image tools with no visual intelligence of their own in a training-free agent loop. Our central claim is about measurement, not intervention: a model that counts by marking leaves a normally hidden serial procedure on the image, and the developmental principles of counting turn those marks into an interpretable audit of serial visual reasoning: every tag is classified against point-level ground truth as on-target, duplicate, phantom, or omitted, the answer is checked against the number of tags, and order irrelevance is tested by forcing opposite traversal orders. Across 9 models, 682 images, and 7 harness conditions we find that (i) the exact-counting range is a model-specific signature spanning nearly two orders of magnitude (R80 from 3 to 150 dots); (ii) as an intervention the finger mostly fails: tags help 4 of 9 models on small-count photographs, hurt imprecise pointers, and rarely beat a verbal routine or a blind point list; what the loop buys is an auditable trace, not accuracy; (iii) as measurement it succeeds: a tag-perturbation probe shows that precise pointers read their answers off the tags, pointing precision tracks which models benefit, dense scenes fail by omission, and models rarely revise after seeing their own tags; and (iv) the capacities dissociate: models follow an instructed traversal order yet often change their answer when it reverses, and children's regular-over-scattered advantage appears only under the routine and survives lattices that defeat a rows-times-columns shortcut.
bullets: Exact-counting ability is model-specific, with the reported R80 range spanning 3–150 dots across 9 models.
Marking items improves counting for only 4 of 9 models on small-count photographs; it can hurt imprecise pointers and rarely outperforms simpler routines.
Tag-level audits classify errors as on-target, duplicate, phantom, or omitted, exposing whether answers are grounded in the visual trace.
Precise pointers tend to derive answers from their tags, while dense scenes primarily cause omissions and models seldom revise after tagging.
Traversal order following, order-invariant counting, and regular-versus-scattered advantages dissociate, indicating multiple underlying counting capacities.

papers.selection_reason: VLM counting evaluation based on spatial marking and ordering is directly relevant to spatial reasoning diagnostics in multimodal large language models.
papers.title: Give the Model a Finger: Developmentally Aligned Evaluation of Counting in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: A developmental counting-inspired tagging procedure reveals that VLMs’ counting failures are mainly serial, omission-prone, and poorly self-corrected, while producing useful auditable traces rather than reliably improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: When does experience memory help a closed-loop LLM driving agent? Published gains cannot say, because the two factors we find to matter most, which warmup experiences the pool contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them. We answer with a controlled evaluation on one audited HighwayEnv testbed (1Hz, gpt-4o-mini for the decisive contrasts). We treat the warmup pool as a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools) and add token-matched irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diagnostics, caution-pricing metrics, and quantified audits of the baseline ports. The probe suite spans flat-text retrieval (a DiLu port), a single-frame grid port (RESPOND-inspired), our episodic temporal-graph memory, a retrieval-free consolidated rulebook, and a flat K-step observation-history baseline. Four findings follow, each a property of this testbed. (1) Headline memory gains belong to the warmup draw. The reported pool is the best of ten for both retrieval memories, which beat No-Memory in only one pool of ten (sign test p=0.011), and even the rulebook's apparent pool-immunity collapsed on five fresh draws. (2) No retrieval design tested exceeds token-matched filler. The collision-only merge ceiling is reached by a single 15-token caution instruction, and metrics that price caution erase the rulebook's lead. (3) Representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. (4) Baseline port quality silently inverts conclusions. On this testbed, a single-pool comparison without filler controls would have reported memory gains that these controls reverse. We release the testbed, audited ports, seeds, and caches.
bullets: Memory gains were highly sensitive to which warmup experiences were sampled: retrieval systems beat No-Memory in only 1 of 10 pools.
A single 15-token caution instruction matched the collision-only benefit of retrieval, and caution-aware metrics removed the rulebook’s apparent lead.
More sophisticated memory representations showed no robust advantage in this evaluation.
Baseline implementation quality and uncontrolled prompts could reverse the reported conclusion about whether memory helps.
The study releases the testbed, audited ports, random seeds, and caches; findings are scoped to this testbed and decisive model setting.

papers.title: When Does Experience Memory Help Closed-Loop LLM Driving Agents? A Controlled Evaluation with Resampled Warmup Pools, Token-Matched Fillers, and Audited Baselines
papers.tldr: In one audited HighwayEnv testbed, apparent benefits from experience memory in closed-loop LLM driving agents largely vanish under resampled warmup pools and token-matched filler controls.

papers.abstract: System One models produce probabilistic judgments that software can consume directly, making reliable confidence as important as answer accuracy. Yet joint training across text, images, and video remains underexplored, and the contributions of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions (RLCD) are difficult to separate. We introduce UniJev, a trimodal framework that scores candidate answers with a shared head under joint supervised training across text, images, and video. Supervised decision models improve accuracy over their backbone readouts across all three modalities, while the existing RLCD algorithms change accuracy little and have inconsistent effects on visual calibration across recipes. These findings motivate a separate supervised objective for confidence calibration. We introduce Cora (Confidence--Outcome Reliability Alignment), which groups current predictions by confidence and optimizes each prediction's confidence toward the empirical accuracy of its bin. At both 2B and 9B, Cora lowers image and video expected calibration error (ECE) while preserving accuracy, without a reinforcement stage. We release our code at https://github.com/wjnwjnwj/UniJev.
bullets: Joint supervised training improves answer accuracy across text, images, and video compared with backbone readouts.
Existing reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions has little effect on accuracy and inconsistent effects on visual calibration.
Cora calibrates confidence by aligning binned predictions with their empirical accuracy.
At both 2B and 9B, Cora lowers image and video ECE while preserving accuracy, without reinforcement training.
The study focuses on text-image-video System One decision models and releases its code publicly.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems built from frozen language models communicate through text, which discards the internal state the sender already computed and makes the receiver pay to rebuild it. Work on internal channels avoids that cost, framing the problem as transfer: agent A sends information to agent B. Every agent pair that must communicate needs its own transfer bridge, and every agent added to a system needs a new bridge fitted against each previous agent. We reframe this problem as sharing: an agent publishes its internal state once into a pool, and every peer reads that pool through a single mechanism fitted to no sender in particular, so adding an agent adds a publisher and no new bridge. Whereas the carrier of the internal state and the fusion mechanism are usually chosen independently in the literature, our main finding is that these two choices are coupled; the deciding factor is where the carrier enters the receiver's computation. Consumability is a property of the receiving computation rather than of the representation. We find that the key-value (KV) cache must be augmented rather than swapped in: the receiver cross-attends over a peer's cache while keeping its own, and with only a small query-side adapter trained, matches the accuracy it gets from reading the source document. Activations invert this. They are best written straight into the receiver, with no bridge, no adapter and no training, which beats exposing them alongside the receiver's own, though that advantage rests on knowing where in the receiver the state belongs. The rule is augment the KV cache, replace the activation, established under one protocol with a shared control ladder. One adapter, trained once, also serves publishers it never trained on, and a pool of several at once, but only those whose internal state lies close to the receiver's own.
bullets: Reframes multi-agent internal communication as shared publishing to a common pool, avoiding pair-specific transfer bridges.
Shows that carrier and fusion mechanism are coupled through where peer state enters the receiver’s computation.
KV-cache sharing works by cross-attending to peer keys and values while preserving the receiver’s own cache, using only a small query-side adapter.
Activation sharing works best by directly writing into the receiver, without a bridge, adapter, or training.
A single adapter generalizes to unseen publishers and multiple pooled agents when their states are sufficiently close to the receiver’s.

papers.abstract: Activation steering adds a vector to a model's hidden states to control a named behaviour. A gain on that behaviour, however, does not show that the vector controls it directly: it may act through a component shared with neighbouring behaviours, which unsteered and random baselines cannot separate. We introduce the competing-target test: a vector is compared with the vector built the same way for a competing target, and an equivalence test states when their difference is below a useful margin. We apply it in open-weight models to vectors for Kantian deontology, which judges an act by the rule it follows, and act utilitarianism, which judges it by the welfare it produces. On held-out situations, prompting a framework raises its score and lowers the other's, whereas vectors for either framework move both scores alike, and none reaches the margin. The two vectors share most of their direction, a request to apply some framework; the same construction separates an optimistic from a pessimistic tone, whose vectors share much less. What a vector shares with its competitors therefore sets what it controls: steering a perspective can deliver a mixture, and measuring a disposition can measure its neighbours, unless tested against the competing target.
bullets: A gain on the intended behaviour may reflect components shared with competing behaviours.
The competing-target test compares a steering vector with one constructed for its competing target and checks whether their difference exceeds a useful margin.

The ethical vectors share most of their direction, unlike optimistic and pessimistic tone vectors, which are more distinct.
Steering vectors may therefore produce mixtures of perspectives and require competing-target evaluation to establish specificity.

papers.abstract: 3D semantic occupancy prediction is crucial for autonomous driving, but camera-based methods degrade in low-light conditions and LiDAR-based methods are sensitive to adverse weather. 4D radar is more robust, yet its sparsity and the high cost of radar tensor processing limit its use. We propose Radar Geometric-Semantic Occupancy Prediction (RadarGSOcc), an efficient framework that directly processes 4D radar tensors by separately extracting geometric and semantic features, including Doppler information, with a deformable attention-based geometric refinement module as its key component. We also introduce the K-Radar 3DSemOcc benchmark, the first large-scale benchmark for 3D semantic occupancy prediction using 4D radar tensors, built on the K-Radar dataset with refined LiDAR-based annotations. RadarGSOcc predicts 15 classes within a 51.2m range and achieves 38.2% IoU, 7.6% mIoU, and 25.5% weighted mIoU, outperforming RadarOcc by 17% relative (25.5 vs. 21.9) in weighted mIoU while using fewer parameters and lower computation. It substantially improves truck prediction while trading off car accuracy, outperforms camera-based approaches, and narrows the gap with LiDAR-based methods. To assess robustness without per-frame ground truth in adverse weather, we further propose a novel proxy metric, Environment-Based KL Divergence (EBKL), under which 4D radar proves a reliable and efficient modality for 3D semantic occupancy prediction. The dataset and code will be publicly available.
bullets: Addresses camera degradation in low light and LiDAR sensitivity to adverse weather, while tackling 4D radar sparsity and processing cost.

papers.abstract: Local learning reduces cross-layer training dependencies, but an efficient accelerator must still retain operands, accumulate gradients, and select quantization scales. We present an FPGA system that trains a CNN and its regional auxiliary classifiers using a shared integer matrix engine. Compact errors are expanded on chip, gradients are folded tile by tile, and historical scales permit direct output conversion. At 200 MHz, the KV260 prototype achieves 76.57% accuracy on CIFAR-10 and 91.85% on SVHN at approximately 4.20 W mean module power. Effective matrix throughput is 31.22 and 31.57 GMAC/s, respectively. Against the same integer method on Jetson Orin Nano, measured training energy is 40.4% and 42.1% lower, with $1.86\times$ and $1.82\times$ longer runtime; measurements use the respective platform power domains. Selected state checks and matching complete-run prediction counts support functional agreement with the software reference.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied agents must maintain task-relevant information, coordinate heterogeneous robots, and adapt their decisions as execution unfolds. Existing benchmarks investigate dynamic task execution and embodied multi-agent coordination, but provide limited evaluation of their intersection. We introduce MAGMA-Bench, an architecture-agnostic benchmark for persistent task reasoning in dynamic multi-robot environments. MAGMA-Bench evaluates agents across increasing task horizons and controlled online perturbations, including execution failures, task interruptions, and mission updates, with scenarios requiring coordination across robots with heterogeneous capabilities. It uses a structured skill-level interface to separate task-level reasoning from perception and low-level control. We evaluate locally deployable open-weight planners, multi-agent state-tracking strategies, and frontier models. Even the strongest evaluated models fail on a substantial fraction of clean episodes, and their success rates decrease further under online perturbations. Supervised adaptation greatly improves a small model, but performance remains substantially lower on longer and multi-robot missions. We release the benchmark, 261,646 task-level training examples, and an architecture-agnostic expert-trace generation pipeline.
bullets: Tests increasing task horizons with execution failures, interruptions, and mission updates.
Uses a structured skill-level interface to isolate task reasoning from perception and low-level control.

Even strong models fail often on clean tasks, with performance declining further under perturbations and longer missions.

papers.abstract: RGB-D semantic segmentation has made notable progress by fusing RGB and Depth, yet mainstream models still learn features almost exclusively from pixel-level supervision, lacking direct high-level semantic constraints. This raises a central question-can external knowledge such as language priors inject stronger semantic discriminability into mainstream RGB-D segmentation models. We present DTFormer, a novel tri-modal (RGB-D-Text) semantic segmentation framework. At its core is Text-guided Semantic Alignment Module (TSAM) that first encodes textual cues into a set of semantic prototypes and then explicitly aligns multi-modal RGB-D features with these prototypes at multiple encoder and decoder layers. This design imposes strong semantic regularization on representation learning, guiding the network toward more discriminative features. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show that DTFormer delivers consistent gains while remaining simple and efficient. Our results demonstrate that explicit semantic alignment offers an effective and practical route to improving RGB-D semantic segmentation. The code will be released upon acceptance.
bullets: Addresses the lack of high-level semantic constraints in pixel-supervised RGB-D segmentation.
Introduces a tri-modal RGB-D-Text framework with a Text-guided Semantic Alignment Module (TSAM).
TSAM encodes text into semantic prototypes and aligns multi-modal features at multiple encoder and decoder layers.
Experiments on multiple benchmarks show consistent gains with a simple and efficient design.
The approach demonstrates that explicit language-based semantic alignment can strengthen feature discriminability.

papers.abstract: We investigate the problem of role-capability leakage (RCL), in which a role-prompted reasoning model generates convincing in-role text while continuing to exhibit capabilities on benchmarks that exceed those implied by the assigned role. For example, when a model is prompted to assume the role of a kindergarten student, one might expect its performance on a mathematics benchmark to reflect kindergarten-level ability rather than expert-level proficiency in solving calculus problems. We introduce RoleCapBench, a curriculum-grounded benchmark for evaluating RCL across six educational roles and four assessment levels spanning elementary school through A-level, and use it to evaluate three open-weight reasoning models. We find that although the models can generate stylistically convincing in-role responses, they consistently fail to align their underlying capabilities with their assigned roles. Naive role prompting yields strong role-voice scores of 1.218--1.389 while retaining above-role accuracy of 0.811--0.898. RCL persists across a range of prompting conditions, including prompts that explicitly instruct the model to match the role's capability level. To mitigate this problem, we propose Injection, an inference-time intervention that combines explicit, role-specific capability guidelines with a guiding prefilled response prefix. Injection improves role-capability alignment across models, reducing above-role accuracy by up to 0.562 while preserving in-role accuracy with a marginal drop of less than 0.058 across most models. All artifacts, including scripts and evaluation data, will be released upon acceptance.

papers.abstract: Training a visuomotor policy calls for abundant demonstrations that closely match the target environment, yet collecting them anew remains expensive. Existing demonstration synthesis methods reduce this cost but remain constrained by high manual effort, limited visual fidelity, or heavy reliance on physics simulators. This paper introduces GaussianFactory, a high-fidelity data engine that mass-produces demonstrations with a single video scan as its only human input and no physics engine in the generation loop. Specifically, GaussianFactory reconstructs the scene as an editable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) replica and samples from the object-combination tasks the scene affords. For each task, it plans grasps and trajectories purely kinematically on the geometric reconstruction, rendering photorealistic demonstrations that visually match the target environment. Physical dynamics enter the pipeline only where contact force interactions dictate the outcome---during grasp formation, via a learned contact model pretrained once on an interaction dataset. To evaluate the downstream utility of the synthesized demonstrations, we implement an end-to-end scan-to-deployment workflow in two setups: a simulated scene that stands in for the real world to enable reproducibility, and a real-world workspace with a physical UR10e robot. In each setup, a standard diffusion policy trained solely on the synthesized demonstrations achieves 95.1% and 84.2% success rates, respectively.

papers.abstract: Learning in robotic games is constrained not only by strategic information but also by what the body can still execute. We study this coupling in a hierarchical humanoid-quadruped penalty system in which game-level self-play policies command fixed soccer whole-body controllers (S-WBCs). The humanoid shooting skill is initialized from self-collected motion-capture data, whereas the quadruped saving skill is learned by reinforcement learning. We introduce dynamics-induced commitment mapping (DIC-Map), a body-grounded analysis that estimates continuation capability, identifies the first persistent loss of a terminal alternative, and tests whether the remaining interaction admits a reduced zero-sum game. For symmetric terminal alternatives, the reduced game yields a closed-form bound on optimal strategy concentration determined by the responder's value of deferring. We further show that, when the responder acts through an estimator, equal response values eliminate the direct terminal-allocation gradient and leave an estimator-mediated first-order learning channel. Experiments locate commitment about 0.29 s before contact, and changing only ball speed shifts deferral coverage. Across four responder policies, replacing the estimator raises save rate from 0.240 to 0.472, whereas a comparable gain in read accuracy obtained by waiting raises it only to 0.246. Posterior analysis is used for the equilibrium comparison because the available coverage terms are observational proxies. Project website: https://chris-ruizegeng.github.io/penaltykick/

papers.abstract: Temporary obstacles that may block a robot's planned route create a sequential navigation problem: a robot must decide whether to wait for a blockage to clear, reroute, or acquire more information about the obstacle before acting. We formulate graph navigation among temporary obstacles as a partially observable semi-Markov decision process and introduce SPARROW, a belief-space planner built on Partially Observable Monte Carlo Planning (POMCP). SPARROW searches over traversal, observation, and finite-duration waiting actions while maintaining a particle belief over latent obstacle classes and clearance times. Class-conditioned survival models are learned online from both clearance observations and right-censored encounters where the robot reroutes before clearance is observed. A generative model simulates obstacle arrivals and clearances as each action unfolds, so the planner can account for blockages that may occur along alternative routes. We further introduce a value-of-learning criterion that trades the immediate cost of collecting labelled survival data against its expected reduction in future navigation regret. Across two simulation graphs and multiple obstacle-class settings, SPARROW reduces mean time-to-goal by 12-26% relative to OSCAR, a recent survival-based method for the same problem. On a physical mobile robot, SPARROW reduces mean time-to-goal by 20.5% relative to OSCAR while selectively observing, waiting, and rerouting as environment conditions change.

papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) perform well on complex question answering but often show a reasoning gap, where explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reduces accuracy compared to direct answers. We hypothesize that long reasoning sequences shift attention away from the audio input. To address this, we propose SPARE (Semantic Prediction for Audio REasoning), which introduces a register token aligned with the final conclusion using a cosine similarity loss with a Sentence-BERT embedding. This conditions the model's latent space with the target semantic goal before reasoning begins. Experiments on MMAU and MMAR with SALMONN show improved zero-shot reasoning and stronger early attention to audio without additional inference cost.

papers.abstract: Deepresearch (DR) agents interact with real-world web environments through multi-turn search and visit, causing their contexts to grow rapidly over time. We observe that, even after DR Agentic Reinforcement Learning (DR-RL), 61.6% of the model's remaining prediction errors can still be attributed to insufficient long-context understanding, including longcontext hallucination and failures in cross-document evidence integration. It motivates us to further break the bottleneck of DR-RL by strengthening the model's long-context ability. However, effective LongContext training requires more than simply increasing context length. To bridge the data gap, we propose `DR Rollouts to LongContext-QA (DR-to-Long)'. The method repurposes DR-RL trajectories, which naturally contain search histories, visited webpages, evidence snippets, and final-answer supervision. It then replaces the compact snippets and webpage summaries in each trajectory with the full contents of their corresponding URLs, producing substantially longer multi-document contexts while preserving the original evidence relationships. Building on DR-to-Long, we introduce DLD (DR -> LongQA -> DR)-RL. DLD-RL first performs a short DR-RL stage to collect rollout trajectories, which are then converted into LongQA instances at zero annotation cost. The model is subsequently optimized with LongQA-RL to strengthen LongContext ability, followed by full DR-RL to continue improving its DR capability. Experiments show that DLD-RL outperforms standard DR-RL by 7.3% on three Deepresearch benchmarks and improves performance by 13.5% on three long-context benchmarks.
